claims.text: Controlled additions of Y and Hf induce lattice distortion in NiCoCrAl-based multiprincipal-element alloys.
Y- and Hf-induced lattice distortion raises vacancy formation energies.
Higher vacancy formation energies suppress diffusion of key alloying elements, especially Al.
Al diffusion supplies material necessary for oxide-scale growth.
Y segregates to the metal/oxide interface.
Interfacial Y segregation promotes formation of Y2O3.
Interfacial Y2O3 acts as a diffusion barrier.
Reduced Al mobility limits the supply available for continuous oxide-scale growth.
The combined lattice-distortion and Y2O3 mechanisms slow thermally grown oxide growth.
The combined mechanisms minimize oxide-scale spallation.
Reduced oxide growth and spallation maintain material integrity during prolonged high-temperature exposure.
Higher Y and Hf levels will produce a significantly lower oxidation rate than the baseline alloy.
Higher Y and Hf levels will produce thinner thermally grown oxide layers than the baseline alloy.
Higher Y and Hf levels will produce more adherent oxide scales than the baseline alloy.
Higher Y and Hf levels will produce less spallation than the baseline alloy.
Minimal Y and Hf additions correspond to minimal lattice distortion and reactive-element effects.
The proposed behavior should hold in NiCoCrAl-based multiprincipal-element alloys oxidized in dry air at 1200 °C for up to 500 hours.

contradictions.description: The mechanism specifies lattice distortion and interfacial Y2O3 as parallel contributors, but the falsification rule says that failure to produce significant lattice-distortion differences alone would falsify the hypothesis, even if the independent Y2O3 pathway formed and improved oxidation behavior.
